## Calculations and interpretation

```{r}
# c(): combines values into a vector, converting them to a common type when needed.
# qnorm(): returns a normal lower-tail quantile; sd is standard deviation, not variance.
# kable(): formats a data frame or matrix as a readable report table; digits sets displayed precision.
# data.frame(): builds a table whose named columns have compatible lengths.
# qt(): returns a t lower-tail quantile; df sets degrees of freedom, n-1 for a one-sample mean interval.
# sqrt(): returns the nonnegative square root of a nonnegative number.
# Compare confidence levels with the same fixed summaries.
# Each row gives its own lower-tail critical value and corresponding endpoints.
level <- c(.95,.99)
z <- qnorm(1-(1-level)/2)
knitr::kable(data.frame(level=level, lower=82-z*2, upper=82+z*2, width=2*z*2),digits=3)
level <- c(.95,.90)
t <- qt(1-(1-level)/2,df=69)
se <- 4007/sqrt(70)
knitr::kable(data.frame(level=level, df=69, SE=se, margin=t*se,
 lower=9312-t*se, upper=9312+t*se),digits=3)
```

Lloyd's 99% interval is approximately \$76.85 to \$87.15; it is wider than the 95% interval. The target is mean spending, not a customer's outcome. Household df = 69 and SE is about \$478.92. The 90% interval is narrower than the 95% interval; t accounts for estimating population SD. The confidence claim concerns long-run coverage under repeated sampling. Summaries alone cannot check outliers, population shape, or dependence; the actual sampling and nonresponse mechanisms require design information.
